questions.stemHtml: A 32-year-old man is admitted to the emergency department after an injury to his foot while playing football with his college friends. An MRI examination reveals multiple tendinous tears (see figure). Which of the following bones is associated with the muscle tears?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Calcaneus


The calcaneus is the bone most commonly associated with the tendinous tears seen in this type of injury. The tendo calcaneus, also known as the Achilles tendon, attaches to the calcaneus. The Achilles tendon is the strongest tendon in the body and is responsible for plantarflexion of the foot. Injuries like tendon tears are common in sports-related activities, such as football, where sudden force or trauma is applied to the foot, leading to damage at the site of the calcaneal attachment.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Navicular: The navicular bone is located on the medial side of the foot and is not associated with the Achilles tendon or the tendinous tears described in this case.

 

Option B. Cuboid: The cuboid bone is located on the lateral side of the foot and plays a role in the stability of the lateral foot arch. However, it is not associated with the Achilles tendon or the muscle tears described.

 

Option D. Talus: The talus bone primarily participates in ankle articulation and is not connected to the tendons of the posterior leg muscles responsible for the injury in this scenario.

 

Educational objective:


The calcaneus is the bone associated with the tendo calcaneus (Achilles tendon), making it the most likely bone involved in cases of tendinous tears in the posterior leg.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old man is admitted to the emergency department with a cold and pale foot. Physical examination reveals that the patient suffers from peripheral vascular disease and his popliteal artery is occluded, with no pulse felt upon palpation. What is the landmark to feel the pulse of the femoral artery?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Femoral triangle


The femoral artery pulse is best palpated in the femoral triangle. This anatomical region is located in the upper part of the thigh and is bordered by the inguinal ligament superiorly, the sartorius muscle laterally, and the adductor longus muscle medially. The femoral triangle is where the femoral artery can be felt as it runs superficial and is easily accessible for palpation. In cases of popliteal artery occlusion, assessing the femoral artery pulse at this landmark is crucial.

 

The site to palpate the pulse is immediately below the midpoint of the inguinal ligament, Inguinal ligament extends from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to the pubic tubercle.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Adductor canal: This canal is located distally in the thigh and is where the femoral artery passes deep toward the popliteal fossa. It is not typically used as a site for palpating the femoral artery pulse.

 

Option C. Popliteal fossa: This region is located behind the knee and is used for palpating the popliteal artery, not the femoral artery. Since the popliteal artery is occluded in this patient, it would not be a useful site for palpation in this case.

 

Option D. Inguinal canal: The inguinal canal is a passage in the lower abdomen, located above the femoral triangle. It is not related to the femoral artery and is not a site where the femoral artery pulse can be palpated.

 

Educational objective:


The femoral triangle is the key landmark for palpating the femoral artery pulse, particularly in cases of vascular issues such as popliteal artery occlusion.

questions.stem: During cardiac catheterization of a 6-year-old child, the radiologist notes that the contrast medium released into the arch of the aorta is visible immediately in the left pulmonary artery. What is the most likely explanation for this finding?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Patent ductus arteriosus

 

The patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) is a condition in which the ductus arteriosus, a vessel that connects the pulmonary artery to the aorta during fetal life, remains open after birth. This persistent connection allows blood to flow directly from the aorta into the pulmonary artery. During cardiac catheterization, if contrast medium is injected into the aorta and is seen immediately in the left pulmonary artery, it indicates the presence of a PDA, as the contrast flows through this abnormal connection.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Atrial septal defect: This defect involves a hole in the wall separating the atria of the heart. It would not cause immediate flow of contrast from the aorta to the pulmonary artery.

 

Option C. Patent ductus venosus: This is an abnormality in which the ductus venosus remains open after birth, allowing blood to bypass the liver. It does not affect the connection between the aorta and pulmonary artery.

 

Option D. Ventricular septal defect: This defect involves a hole between the ventricles of the heart, which would cause abnormal blood flow between the ventricles, not between the aorta and pulmonary artery.

 

Educational objective:
 

Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) is characterized by an abnormal connection between the aorta and the pulmonary artery, allowing immediate passage of contrast from the aorta into the pulmonary artery during imaging procedures.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old girl is admitted to the hospital with severe dyspnea. Physical examination reveals that the patient is suffering from an asthma attack, with associated bronchospasm. Which of the following nerves is responsible for the innervation of the bronchial smooth muscle cells?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Vagus


The vagus nerve is responsible for parasympathetic innervation of the bronchial smooth muscles. During an asthma attack, the bronchial smooth muscles undergo contraction, leading to bronchospasm. The vagus nerve mediates bronchoconstriction by releasing acetylcholine, which acts on muscarinic receptors in the bronchial smooth muscle, causing them to contract. This parasympathetic activity increases in conditions like asthma, leading to the symptoms of dyspnea and bronchospasm.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Greater thoracic splanchnic: This nerve provides sympathetic innervation to the abdominal organs, not the lungs, and does not directly influence bronchial smooth muscle tone.

 

Option B. Phrenic: The phrenic nerve innervates the diaphragm, the major muscle involved in breathing, but it does not innervate the bronchial smooth muscles or cause bronchoconstriction.

 

Option D. Lesser thoracic splanchnic: This nerve also provides sympathetic innervation to the abdominal organs, and it does not play a role in the bronchial smooth muscle innervation.

 

Educational objective:


The vagus nerve provides parasympathetic innervation to the bronchial smooth muscles, causing bronchoconstriction during an asthma attack.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old male who fell from a tree complains of severe pain over the right side of his chest due to a rib fracture at the midaxillary line. He is admitted to the hospital with difficulty breathing. Radiographic and physical examinations reveal atelectasis resulting from the accumulation of blood in his pleural space, causing a hemothorax. What is the most likely source of bleeding causing the hemothorax?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Intercostal vessels


The most likely source of bleeding in a hemothorax due to a rib fracture at the midaxillary line is the intercostal vessels. These vessels run along the inferior margin of each rib, within the intercostal spaces. When a rib fracture occurs, particularly in the midaxillary region, the intercostal vessels can be damaged, leading to blood accumulation in the pleural space, resulting in a hemothorax. The proximity of these vessels to the ribs makes them highly susceptible to injury during fractures.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Left common carotid artery: This artery is located in the neck and supplies blood to the head and brain. It is not involved in injuries to the chest and would not cause a hemothorax.

 

Option C. Pulmonary arteries: These arteries supply blood to the lungs. While damage to the pulmonary arteries can cause bleeding, they are less likely to be affected by a rib fracture at the midaxillary line, which more commonly affects the intercostal vessels.

 

Option D. Internal thoracic artery: The internal thoracic artery runs along the inner surface of the anterior chest wall, near the sternum. It is not commonly injured in rib fractures located at the midaxillary line.

 

Educational objective:


The intercostal vessels are the most likely source of bleeding in a hemothorax caused by a rib fracture, particularly at the midaxillary line, due to their close proximity to the ribs.

questions.stem: Fusion of the caudal portions of the kidneys during embryonic development is most likely to result in which of the following congenital conditions?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Horseshoe kidney


During embryonic development, the horseshoe kidney occurs when the caudal (lower) portions of the kidneys fuse together, forming a U-shaped structure. This congenital anomaly prevents the normal ascent of the kidneys, as the fused kidney gets trapped under the inferior mesenteric artery around the L3 level. Although the kidneys function normally in most cases, the abnormal shape and position can lead to complications such as increased risk for kidney stones and urinary tract infections.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Bicornuate uterus: This is a malformation of the uterus in which the uterus is divided into two horns due to incomplete fusion of the paramesonephric ducts, and it is unrelated to kidney development.

 

Option B. Cryptorchidism: This condition refers to undescended testes and is related to testicular development rather than kidney fusion.

 

Option D. Renal agenesis: This condition occurs when one or both kidneys fail to develop entirely, which is distinct from the fusion of kidneys seen in horseshoe kidney formation.

 

Educational objective:


A horseshoe kidney results from the fusion of the caudal portions of the kidneys during embryonic development, leading to abnormal positioning and potential complications.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old male is admitted to the emergency department with severe upper abdominal pain. Gastroscopy reveals a tumor in the antrum of the stomach. A CT scan is ordered to evaluate lymphatic drainage of the stomach. Which of the following lymph nodes is most likely to be involved in a malignancy of the stomach?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Celiac


The celiac lymph nodes are the primary lymph nodes involved in the drainage of the stomach, particularly in the case of malignancy in the antrum. The celiac nodes receive lymphatic drainage from most of the stomach, including the antrum, and are the first nodes likely to be involved in cases of gastric cancer. Tumors in this region frequently spread to these lymph nodes first because of their close proximity to the celiac trunk, which supplies the stomach.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Superior mesenteric: The superior mesenteric nodes drain portions of the small intestine and parts of the colon but are not primarily involved in the drainage of the stomach.

 

Option C. Inferior mesenteric: These nodes drain the large intestine, particularly the distal colon and rectum, and are not relevant to the lymphatic drainage of the stomach.

 

Option D. Hepatic: Although hepatic nodes may be involved in advanced stages of gastric cancer, they are not typically the primary site for lymphatic drainage from the stomach.

 

Educational objective:


The celiac lymph nodes are the primary nodes involved in the lymphatic drainage of the stomach, particularly in malignancies affecting the antrum.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male entered the emergency department with a complaint of severe abdominal pain. During physical examination, it is observed that his cremasteric reflex is absent. Which of the following nerves is responsible for the efferent limb of the cremasteric reflex?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Genitofemoral


The genitofemoral nerve is responsible for the efferent limb of the cremasteric reflex. This reflex involves two components: the afferent limb (sensory) and the efferent limb (motor). The afferent limb is mediated by the ilioinguinal nerve, while the efferent limb is controlled by the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve, which innervates the cremaster muscle. When the inner thigh is stroked, the sensory input from the ilioinguinal nerve triggers a response through the genitofemoral nerve, causing the cremaster muscle to contract, elevating the testis. In the case of an absent cremasteric reflex, there is usually an issue with the genitofemoral nerve or L1-L2 spinal segments.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Ilioinguinal: The ilioinguinal nerve provides sensory input (afferent limb) for the cremasteric reflex but does not control the motor response (efferent limb)

 

Option B. Iliohypogastric: This nerve supplies the lower abdominal muscles and skin, but it does not participate in the cremasteric reflex.

 

Option D. Pudendal: The pudendal nerve innervates the perineum and external genitalia, but it is not involved in the cremasteric reflex.

 

Educational objective:
 

The genitofemoral nerve controls the efferent (motor) limb of the cremasteric reflex, resulting in contraction of the cremaster muscle when the inner thigh is stimulated.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old patient is admitted to the hospital after suffering a ruptured spleen in a skiing accident. Physical examination reveals intense pain that radiates to the region of the left shoulder, presumably due to irritation of the diaphragm. Which of the following signs best describes this condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Kerh sign


Kerh sign refers to referred pain in the left shoulder due to irritation of the diaphragm, often caused by blood or other irritants in the abdominal cavity, such as in cases of a ruptured spleen. The diaphragm is supplied by phrenic nerve (root value - C3, C4 and C5) and the shoulder region is supplied by supraclavicular nerve (root value - C3 and C4). Due to the common C3 and C4 root values the pain get irradiate to shoulder region from the diaphragm. When the diaphragm is irritated, pain signals are referred to the left shoulder, manifesting as Kerh sign, a classic indicator of splenic rupture or irritation.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Mittelschmerz: This is a term used to describe ovulation pain (mid cycle pain), typically experienced as lower abdominal pain, unrelated to diaphragm irritation.

 

Option C. Rovsing sign: This refers to pain in the right lower abdomen when the left side is palpated, often associated with appendicitis, and is not related to diaphragm irritation or shoulder pain.

 

Option D. Psoas sign: This sign indicates irritation of the psoas muscle, often seen in cases of appendicitis, and is unrelated to shoulder pain or diaphragm irritation.

 

Educational objective:


Kerh sign is a clinical indicator of referred left shoulder pain due to diaphragmatic irritation, typically seen in cases of splenic injury or rupture.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man is admitted to the hospital due to severe back pain. Radiographic examination reveals severe osteoporosis of the vertebral column, with crush fractures of vertebrae L4 and L5. Which of the following parts of the vertebrae are most likely to be fractured in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Vertebral bodies


In cases of osteoporosis, the vertebral bodies are the most commonly affected parts of the vertebrae. Osteoporosis leads to a loss of bone density, making the vertebral bodies vulnerable to compression and crush fractures, especially in the lumbar region (L4 and L5). The vertebral bodies bear the majority of the weight and pressure in the spine, and their weakened state in osteoporosis makes them prone to collapse under this pressure, leading to severe pain and deformity.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Spinal process: The spinous processes, located at the back of the vertebrae, are less likely to fracture under the compressive forces typically seen in osteoporosis.

 

Option C. Transverse process: The transverse processes are lateral projections from the vertebrae and are not commonly affected by the compressive forces that cause vertebral body fractures.

 

Option D. Intervertebral disk: While the intervertebral disks can degenerate with age, they do not fracture in the way that bones do. The main issue in osteoporosis is with the bones, not the disks.

 

Educational objective:


Osteoporosis primarily weakens the vertebral bodies, leading to crush fractures, especially in the lumbar region,

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman is admitted to the emergency department after a car crash. Radiographic examination reveals a whiplash injury in addition to hyperextension of her cervical spine. Which of the following ligaments will most likely be injured?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Anterior longitudinal ligament

 

In a whiplash injury, where there is hyperextension of the cervical spine, the anterior longitudinal ligament is most likely to be injured. This ligament runs along the anterior surface of the vertebral bodies and functions to prevent excessive extension. Hyperextension occurs when the head and neck are forcibly thrown backward, as often happens in car accidents, stretching the anterior longitudinal ligament. This ligament is particularly vulnerable to damage in these situations because it is responsible for controlling extension movement.

 

This injury often occurs due to the sudden and forceful backward motion of the head and neck in car crashes, which stresses the anterior longitudinal ligament and can cause it to stretch or tear.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Ligamentum flavum: This ligament is located on the posterior side of the vertebrae and helps resist hyperflexion (forward bending), not hyperextension. Therefore, it is not typically injured in hyperextension injuries.

 

Option C. Posterior longitudinal ligament: This ligament runs along the posterior surface of the vertebral bodies and also helps to prevent hyperflexion. Since hyperextension stretches the spine backward, this ligament is not likely to be injured in this type of injury.

 

Option D. Anulus fibrosus: This is the outer layer of the intervertebral disc, and while it provides structural support to the disc, it is not the primary structure affected during hyperextension injuries like whiplash.

 

Educational objective:

 

In cases of hyperextension injuries, such as those seen in whiplash, the anterior longitudinal ligament is the most likely ligament to be injured due to its role in resisting excessive backward movement of the spine.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man was admitted to the emergency department after he was struck by an automobile. Radiographic examination revealed a fracture through the crista galli of the anterior cranial fossa, resulting in slow, local bleeding. Which of the following is the most likely source of bleeding?

options.label: B
options.text: The great cerebral vein of Galen

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Superior sagittal sinus

 

A fracture through the crista galli of the anterior cranial fossa can result in damage to the superior sagittal sinus, leading to slow and localized bleeding. The crista galli is located near the falx cerebri, where the superior sagittal sinus runs along its superior border. Any trauma to this region can affect the sinus, which is a major venous structure draining blood from the brain and its meninges. The attachment of the falx cerebri to the crista galli explains why this venous sinus is the most likely source of bleeding in this case.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Middle meningeal artery: This artery is usually implicated in epidural hematomas following fractures of the temporal bone and is not 

associated with the crista galli region.
Option B. The great cerebral vein of Galen: This vein is located in the posterior part of the brain and drains deep cerebral structures, making it an unlikely source of bleeding in the anterior cranial fossa.
 

Option D. Superior ophthalmic vein: This vein drains the orbit and enters the cavernous sinus, far from the crista galli, making it an improbable source of bleeding in this scenario.

 

Educational objective:

 

Fractures of the crista galli are likely to cause bleeding from the superior sagittal sinus due to its proximity to the falx cerebri attachment.

The image displays craniorachischisis, a severe congenital anomaly resulting from the failure of the neural tube to close completely. This condition is characterized by the open exposure of both the brain (anencephaly) and spinal cord (rachischisis). Craniorachischisis involves both the head and the spine, leading to an open neural defect. The absence of a formed skull and spine in the image indicates the presence of both anencephaly and rachischisis, The failure of the neural tube to close during early development results in the exposure of the nervous tissue, leaving the brain and spinal cord vulnerable to damage.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Anencephaly: This condition involves the failure of the cranial portion of the neural tube to close, leading to the absence of major portions of the brain and skull. However, this defect does not involve the spinal cord, as seen in the image.


Option B. Rachischisis: This condition specifically refers to the failure of the spinal portion of the neural tube to close, leading to an exposed spinal cord. However, rachischisis does not affect the brain, distinguishing it from the full-body involvement seen in craniorachischisis.


Option D. Meningoencephalocele: In this condition, a sac-like protrusion of brain tissue and meninges herniates through a defect in the skull. This condition does not involve the entire neural tube and typically presents as a localized defect, unlike the full exposure of both the brain and spine seen in craniorachischisis.

 

Educational objective:

questions.stemHtml: Identify the central sulcus of Rolando:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) B



The central sulcus (CS), also called the sulcus of Rolando, is a significant anatomical feature on the brain's lateral surface. It serves as the dividing line between the frontal lobe and the parietal lobe. It is located between the precentral gyrus (responsible for motor control) and the postcentral gyrus (responsible for sensory functions). In the image, the structure labeled B represents the central sulcus, 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Precentral Sulcus (PCS): This sulcus lies anterior to the central sulcus and runs parallel to it. It is found just in front of the precentral gyrus, which is home to the primary motor cortex. The precentral sulcus is involved in the motor control areas but is not the central sulcus.

 

Option C. Postcentral Sulcus (PostCS): This sulcus is located posterior to the central sulcus, just behind the postcentral gyrus. The postcentral gyrus contains the primary somatosensory cortex, which processes sensory input from the body. Though important for sensory processing, the postcentral sulcus is not the central sulcus.

 

Option D. Lateral Sulcus (Lat. S or Sylvian fissure): This is another important sulcus located on the brain's lateral side. It separates the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes and plays a role in defining language and auditory areas, but it is not related to the division between the motor and sensory areas like the central sulcus.

 

Educational objective:


The central sulcus of Rolando is a major anatomical landmark that separates the motor cortex from the sensory cortex and divides the frontal and parietal lobes.

questions.stem: Your patient has lost the ability to discriminate between two points presented simultaneously to the skin. Your neurological evaluation is most likely to reveal a lesion in the:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Medial lemniscus

 

The loss of two-point discrimination is most likely due to a lesion in the medial lemniscus. The medial lemniscus carries sensory information related to fine touch, vibration, and proprioception from the body to the brain. This pathway includes the fasciculus gracilis and fasciculus cuneatus, which are responsible for transmitting fine touch sensations, including two-point discrimination, to the somatosensory cortex. A lesion in this pathway will impair the brain’s ability to discriminate between two simultaneous points of contact on the skin.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Lateral lemniscus: This structure is part of the auditory pathway and is not involved in somatosensory processing or two-point discrimination.


Option C. Spinal lemniscus: The spinal lemniscus includes the spinothalamic tracts, which are involved in pain and temperature sensation, not fine touch or two-point discrimination.


Option D. Trigeminal lemniscus: This pathway is involved in transmitting sensory information from the face, and while it does carry fine touch information, the question pertains to body sensation, not facial sensation.

 

Educational objective:

 

A lesion in the medial lemniscus can cause the loss of two-point discrimination due to its role in transmitting fine touch and proprioceptive information from the body to the brain.

questions.stem: A transverse section through the brainstem contains the nucleus of Edinger-Westphal. Which other structure are you most likely to see in the same section?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Superior colliculus

 

The nucleus of Edinger-Westphal is part of the oculomotor complex located at the level of the midbrain. Specifically, it is associated with the third cranial nerve (oculomotor nerve), which is found at the level of the superior colliculus. The superior colliculus is responsible for visual reflexes and is located in the dorsal part of the midbrain. Since the Edinger-Westphal nucleus and the superior colliculus are both at this level of the brainstem, they would be present in the same transverse section.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Central canal: The central canal is part of the spinal cord and is not found in the midbrain, where the Edinger-Westphal nucleus is located.
 

Option B. Fourth ventricle: The fourth ventricle is located more caudally, at the level of the pons and medulla, and would not be seen at the level of the midbrain.
 

Option C. Olive: The olive is located in the medulla and is not at the same level as the Edinger-Westphal nucleus, which is in the midbrain.

 

Educational objective:

 

The nucleus of Edinger-Westphal is found in the midbrain at the level of the superior colliculus, making the superior colliculus the structure most likely seen in the same transverse section.

Educational objective: The nucleus of Edinger-Westphal is found in the midbrain at the level of the superior colliculus, making the superior colliculus the structure most likely seen in the same transverse section.

questions.stem: Your patient has a loss of general sensation and ageusia on the posterior one third of the tongue, and touching the lateral wall of the throat fails to elicit a gag reflex. The neural structure that is the most likely to have been lesioned is the:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Glossopharyngeal nerve

 

The glossopharyngeal nerve (cranial nerve IX) is responsible for providing general sensation and taste (ageusia) to the posterior one third of the tongue. It also carries afferent fibers for the gag reflex, which are triggered by touching the lateral wall of the pharynx. A lesion in this nerve would result in the symptoms described: loss of sensation and taste in the posterior one third of the tongue, along with the failure of the gag reflex when the lateral wall of the throat is touched. This makes the glossopharyngeal nerve the most likely structure to be damaged in this case.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Vagus nerve: While the vagus nerve contributes to the motor component of the gag reflex, it is not primarily involved in sensation and taste in the posterior third of the tongue.
 

Option C. Facial nerve: The facial nerve provides taste sensation to the anterior two thirds of the tongue, not the posterior third.
 

Option D. Nucleus ambiguous: This nucleus controls motor function in the pharynx and larynx but is not directly responsible for sensation or taste in the posterior tongue, making it an unlikely cause of these symptoms.

 

Educational objective:

 

The glossopharyngeal nerve is responsible for sensation and taste in the posterior one third of the tongue and is involved in the gag reflex. A lesion in this nerve would result in loss of these functions.

questions.stem: Your patient has a stooped posture, shuffling gait, and a tremor in the fingers at rest. Which part of the brain will show neuronal degeneration?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Mesencephalon

 

The symptoms of a stooped posture, shuffling gait, and resting tremor are characteristic of Parkinson’s disease, which results from degeneration in the substantia nigra. The substantia nigra is located in the mesencephalon (midbrain), and it produces dopamine, which is essential for motor control. When the substantia nigra degenerates, it leads to the hallmark motor symptoms of Parkinson’s, such as bradykinesia, resting tremor, and postural instability.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Metencephalon: This part of the brainstem includes structures such as the pons and cerebellum, which are more involved in coordination and balance, not the motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease.
 

Option B. Diencephalon: This region includes structures such as the thalamus and hypothalamus, which are not primarily involved in the motor control symptoms of Parkinson's disease.
 

Option D. Myelencephalon: This part of the brainstem includes the medulla oblongata and is responsible for autonomic functions such as breathing and heart rate, unrelated to the motor symptoms described here.

 

Educational objective:

 

Parkinson's disease is caused by degeneration in the substantia nigra, located in the mesencephalon, leading to motor symptoms such as a stooped posture, shuffling gait, and resting tremor.

questions.stem: A patient has suffered a stroke caused by occlusion of the right anterior cerebral artery. This patient is most likely to present with:

options.label: A
options.text: A loss of pain and temperature sensations in the left leg

options.label: C
options.text: Drooping of the corner of the mouth on the left

questions.answerText: A loss of pain and temperature sensations in the left leg
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) A loss of pain and temperature sensations in the left leg

 

The right anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial surface of the brain, particularly regions involved in controlling the motor and sensory functions of the lower limbs. Since the sensory and motor pathways cross at the level of the medulla, an occlusion in the right anterior cerebral artery will cause contralateral (left-sided) sensory deficits. The spinothalamic tract, which carries pain and temperature sensations, will be disrupted, leading to a loss of pain and temperature sensation in the left leg. The homunculus, which maps the brain's control of body regions, shows that the lower limbs are controlled by the medial portion of the brain, supplied by the anterior cerebral artery.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Weakness of the right leg: This would occur if the stroke affected the left anterior cerebral artery, as the left hemisphere controls the right side of the body.
 

Option C. Drooping of the corner of the mouth on the left: Facial symptoms like drooping are more commonly associated with strokes in the middle cerebral artery, which controls facial muscles, not the anterior cerebral artery.
 

Option D. A nonfluent aphasia: Broca’s aphasia is associated with damage to Broca's area in the left hemisphere, supplied by the middle cerebral artery, not the anterior cerebral artery.

 

Educational objective:

 

Occlusion of the right anterior cerebral artery results in contralateral sensory and motor deficits, particularly in the left leg, including the loss of pain and temperature sensation.

questions.stem: A lawyer suffers a bad fall that results in head trauma. His motor, sensory, and language skills are intact after the incident, and he has no visual problems. In the following weeks, he begins to lose interest in his work and doesn't seem to care much about his family. The trauma most likely affected the:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Frontal lobe

 

The symptoms described in this case, including a lack of interest in work and decreased care for family members, are indicative of frontal lobe damage. The frontal lobe is responsible for higher cognitive functions such as personality, decision-making, social behavior, and emotional regulation. A traumatic injury to this area can lead to personality changes, social withdrawal, and apathy, all of which are seen in this patient. These symptoms, along with the lack of motor, sensory, and language impairments, point to the prefrontal cortex, a part of the frontal lobe, being affected by the trauma.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Temporal lobe: Damage to the temporal lobe would likely result in memory, language, or hearing problems, none of which are noted in this case.
 

Option B. Parietal lobe: The parietal lobe is involved in processing sensory information and spatial awareness. A lesion here would likely cause sensory or motor deficits, which are not present in this patient.
 

Option C. Occipital lobe: The occipital lobe processes visual information. Since the patient has no visual problems, this lobe is not likely to be affected.

 

Educational objective:

 

A traumatic injury leading to a loss of interest in work, family, and social engagement, without affecting motor or sensory functions, points to damage in the frontal lobe, which controls personality and social behavior.

questions.stem: Which of the following cells are found in the white matter of the spinal cord?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Axons

 

In the white matter of the spinal cord, axons are the primary component. The white matter consists mostly of myelinated axons that form tracts and transmit signals up and down the spinal cord. These axons are covered with a myelin sheath, which gives the white matter its pale appearance. The main role of the white matter is to relay information between different parts of the central nervous system.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Cell bodies: Cell bodies are primarily located in the gray matter, not the white matter. The gray matter contains neurons, which are responsible for processing information.
 

Option C. Dendrites: Dendrites are part of neurons and are mostly found in the gray matter. They receive signals from other neurons but are not prominent in the white matter.
 

Option D. Nissl's granules: Nissl's granules are found in the cell bodies of neurons, which are located in the gray matter. These granules are involved in protein synthesis and are not present in the white matter.

 

Educational objective:

 

The white matter of the spinal cord is primarily composed of axons, which transmit signals between different regions of the nervous system.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the papillae from the given histological section:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Circumvallate

 

The image shows the classic histological structure of circumvallate papillae, which are large, dome-shaped papillae surrounded by a trench-like structure. Circumvallate papillae are found at the back of the tongue and contain numerous taste buds located in the walls of the trench. The trench-like appearance, along with their large size, distinguishes circumvallate papillae from other types. These papillae play an important role in detecting bitter tastes and are associated with Von Ebner’s glands, which secrete a fluid that helps in taste perception.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Fungiform: These papillae are smaller, mushroom-shaped, and are more commonly located at the tip and sides of the tongue. They lack the prominent trench and dome shape seen in circumvallate papillae.
 

Option C. Filiform: Filiform papillae are slender, thread-like, and cover most of the tongue’s surface. They lack taste buds and are primarily involved in mechanical functions.
 

Option D. Foliate: Foliate papillae are located on the lateral sides of the tongue and appear as ridges and grooves. They are not dome-shaped nor do they possess a trench-like structure.

 

Educational objective:

 

Circumvallate papillae are characterized by their large dome shape and a surrounding trench, and they are involved in detecting bitter tastes.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the cell marked in the histological image of the cerebellum shown below:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Purkinje cells

 

The cell marked in the histological image is a Purkinje cell. Purkinje cells are flask-shaped neurons located in the Purkinje layer of the cerebellum. These cells have a large, prominent nucleus and are responsible for transmitting signals to the deep cerebellar nuclei. The Purkinje cell layer is situated between the molecular layer above and the granular layer below. The distinctive flask-shaped structure of these cells makes them easy to identify. 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Basket cells: These are found in the molecular layer and are inhibitory interneurons that form synapses with Purkinje cells, but they are not large or flask-shaped like the marked cell in the image.

 

Option C. Golgi cells: These cells are located in the granular layer, below the Purkinje layer, and serve an inhibitory role on granule cells. However, they are smaller and not flask-shaped like Purkinje cells.

 

Option D. Granule cells: Granule cells are small neurons found in the granular layer, far smaller than Purkinje cells, and do not have the large flask-shaped appearance seen in the image.

 

Educational objective:

 

Purkinje cells are large, flask-shaped neurons located in the Purkinje layer of the cerebellum and are essential for coordinating motor activity.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the type of cartilage shown in the image below:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Elastic cartilage


The image illustrates elastic cartilage, which is distinct due to the presence of a dense network of elastic fibers embedded in the cartilage matrix. Elastic cartilage has the following key characteristics:

It contains chondrocytes (cartilage cells) located within lacunae, similar to other types of cartilage, but it is distinguished by the elastic fibers that surround the chondrocytes.

 

The elastic fibers are visible in the extracellular matrix, providing flexibility and the ability to return to its original shape after deformation.

Elastic cartilage is commonly found in areas of the body where flexible support is required, such as the external ear (auricle), the epiglottis, and certain parts of the larynx. It allows these structures to bend and then resume their shape.

 

Other Options:


Option A. Hyaline cartilage: Hyaline cartilage is the most common type of cartilage. It has a glassy and smooth appearance under a microscope because it lacks visible fibers in the matrix. It is found in the joints (articular cartilage), trachea, nose, and costal cartilage. The absence of prominent fibers in hyaline cartilage distinguishes it from elastic cartilage.

 

Option C. Articular cartilage: This is a specialized form of hyaline cartilage, found at the ends of long bones in synovial joints, providing a smooth surface for movement. While it shares the glassy appearance of hyaline cartilage, it lacks the elastic fibers that define elastic cartilage. Articular cartilage has excellent resistance to wear but lacks flexibility compared to elastic cartilage.

 

Option D. Fibrocartilage: Fibrocartilage is very different in appearance from both hyaline and elastic cartilage. It contains thick bundles of collagen fibers, giving it a dense, fibrous texture under the microscope. It is found in regions that require tough, supportive structures, such as the intervertebral discs, pubic symphysis, and menisci of the knee. The absence of elastic fibers and the presence of collagen bundles set fibrocartilage apart from elastic cartilage.

 

Educational Objective:

 

 

(Mnemonic - ETC NEWS) 

 

E - Ear pinna 

E - Eustachian tube 

E - Epiglottis 

T - Tip of nose 

T - Tip of arytenoid cartilage 

T - Tritiate cartilage 

C - Corniculate 

C - Cuneiform

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is not true about the given Histology?

options.label: A
options.text: The cortical portion is mainly composed of lymphocytes

options.label: C
options.text: It is derived from the fourth Pharyngeal pouch

options.label: D
options.text: It undergoes atrophy from puberty onwards

questions.answerText: It is derived from the fourth Pharyngeal pouch
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) It is derived from the fourth Pharyngeal pouch

 

The structure in question is the thymus, which is derived from the third pharyngeal pouch, not the fourth, as stated in option C. The thymus is a primary lymphoid organ responsible for T-cell maturation. Its cortex is predominantly composed of lymphocytes, while the medulla contains structures known as Hassall's corpuscles. The thymus undergoes gradual atrophy after puberty, which is why it becomes smaller and less active in adults.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. The cortical portion is mainly composed of lymphocytes: This is a true statement. The cortical portion of the thymus is filled with densely packed lymphocytes, a key feature of the organ's immune function.

 

Option B. The medulla contains Hassall's corpuscles: This is also true. Hassall's corpuscles are characteristic structures found in the medulla of the thymus, and they play a role in the regulation of immune function.

 

Option D. It undergoes atrophy from puberty onwards: This is a true statement. After puberty, the thymus begins to atrophy, and its functional capacity diminishes as a person ages.

 

Educational objective:

 

 

The thymus is derived from the third pharyngeal pouch and undergoes atrophy after puberty.

questions.stemHtml: Shown epithelium is found in?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Urinary bladder

 

 

The epithelium shown in the image is transitional epithelium, also known as urothelium. This type of epithelium is found in the urinary bladder. It has a unique structure that allows it to stretch, which is essential for accommodating fluctuations in the volume of urine. The cells are arranged in layers, and the superficial layer consists of large, dome-shaped cells known as "umbrella cells." These cells flatten when the bladder is distended and return to their dome shape when the bladder is empty, allowing the bladder to expand and contract without damaging the tissue.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Stomach: The stomach is lined by simple columnar epithelium, not transitional epithelium. This tissue type does not accommodate stretching like the epithelium in the bladder.

 

Option B. Lungs: The lungs are lined with ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium in the bronchi, and simple squamous epithelium in the alveoli, neither of which resemble the transitional epithelium seen in the bladder.

 

Option C. Liver: The liver is composed of hepatocytes and is not lined by any epithelium resembling that in the image. Its structure is vastly different from transitional epithelium.

 

Educational objective:

 

Transitional epithelium, or urothelium, is found in the urinary bladder and allows for stretching to accommodate urine volume changes.

questions.stem: The movements at the _________________ joint permit a person to look to the right and left.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Atlanto-axial

 

The atlanto-axial joint allows for the rotation of the head, which enables a person to look to the right and left. This joint is formed between the first and second cervical vertebrae (C1 and C2). The atlas (C1) rotates around the dens of the axis (C2), allowing for head rotation. This movement is distinct from the atlanto-occipital joint, which is responsible for the nodding motion 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Atlanto-occipital: This joint is responsible for the nodding "yes" movement and does not permit the rotational movement needed to look left or right.

 

Option C. C2-C3: This joint contributes to general neck movements but does not play a key role in the specific rotation of the head, which is primarily controlled by the atlanto-axial joint.

 

Option D. C3-C4: Like the C2-C3 joint, this joint is involved in neck flexion and extension but does not allow the significant rotational movement controlled by the atlanto-axial joint.

 

Educational objective:

 

The atlanto-axial joint is responsible for allowing rotational movements of the head, enabling a person to look left and right.

questions.stemHtml: A 40-year-old male patient presents with a swelling that has been slowly growing in the past 2 years. On examination, it was variable in consistency and fully mobile. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Parotid tumor

 

The most likely diagnosis is parotid tumor, particularly pleomorphic adenoma. a slowly growing mass, variable in consistency, and fully mobile is characteristic of a parotid tumor. It mentions that this tumor is encapsulated by the parotid fascia, making it mobile. The pleomorphic adenoma is a common benign tumor of the parotid gland, and its slow growth aligns with the patient’s symptoms of a two-year history of gradual enlargement.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Dermoid cyst: Dermoid cysts are typically found in the midline and do not generally grow in the area described for this case. They also do not fit the description of a swelling with variable consistency and mobility.

 

Option C. Sebaceous cyst: Sebaceous cysts are usually smaller, often have a visible punctum, and do not grow as slowly or present with such variable consistency.

 

Option D. Cervical lymph node: Enlarged cervical lymph nodes tend to be firmer and less mobile than a benign parotid tumor. They often grow due to infection or malignancy and do not exhibit the slow, variable growth seen here.

 

Educational objective:

 

A parotid tumor, specifically pleomorphic adenoma, typically presents as a slow-growing, mobile, and variably consistent mass.

questions.stem: A patient presents with sudden onset of chest pain shooting to the neck and interscapular region. X-ray shows widened mediastinum. BP is 110/90 mmHg in the right upper limb and 160/100 mmHg in the left upper limb. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Acute aortic dissection

 

The most likely diagnosis is acute aortic dissection. aortic dissection is characterized by severe chest pain that radiates to the neck and interscapular region, along with a widened mediastinum on X-ray. The difference in blood pressure between the right and left upper limbs is also a classic sign, as aortic dissection can disrupt blood flow to different parts of the body. These symptoms strongly indicate an aortic dissection, which is a medical emergency.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Acute coronary syndrome: While coronary syndrome can cause chest pain, it typically does not cause a significant difference in blood pressure between the limbs or a widened mediastinum on X-ray.

 

Option B. Acute pulmonary embolism: Pulmonary embolism may cause sudden chest pain and breathing difficulty, but it does not usually result in the BP differences or radiating pain to the interscapular region seen in aortic dissection.

 

Option D. Esophageal rupture: Esophageal rupture can cause chest pain and mediastinal widening, but the difference in blood pressure between the limbs points to a vascular cause like aortic dissection.

 

Educational objective:

 

Acute aortic dissection presents with severe chest pain radiating to the neck and interscapular region, a widened mediastinum, and a difference in blood pressure between the upper limbs.

questions.stemHtml: A 50-year-old patient with a history of trauma one week back presents with confusion and ataxia. He is on treatment for alcohol dependence, and his last intake was 2 weeks back. CT scan reveals the following finding. What is the diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Subdural hemorrhage

 

Diagnosis is subdural hemorrhage. subdural hemorrhage presents with a "banana sign" on imaging, and in this case, the patient’s history of trauma, confusion, and ataxia aligns with this diagnosis. Subdural hemorrhages are common in patients with a history of alcohol dependence due to their higher risk of falls and head trauma, and the characteristic presentation seen on the CT scan confirms this diagnosis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Extradural hemorrhage: This type of hemorrhage typically presents with a "lucid interval" following the injury, which is not described in this case.

 

Option C. Intra-parenchymal hemorrhage: While intra-parenchymal hemorrhages may cause confusion, they do not present with the characteristic imaging findings and history seen here.

 

Option D. Subarachnoid hemorrhage: Subarachnoid hemorrhage often presents with a "thunderclap" headache, which is not mentioned in this case. The imaging and clinical history are more indicative of a subdural hemorrhage.

 

Educational objective:

 

Subdural hemorrhage presents with a "banana sign" on imaging and is common in patients with a history of trauma and alcohol dependence.

questions.stemHtml: A 23-year-old male patient presents with midline swelling in the neck. The swelling moves with deglutition and protrusion of the tongue. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Thyroglossal cyst

 

The most likely diagnosis is a thyroglossal cyst. Swellings located in the midline of the neck, which move with deglutition and protrusion of the tongue, are typically related to the thyroglossal duct. The thyroid gland is connected to the base of the tongue through this duct, and any remnants can lead to the formation of a thyroglossal cyst. The cyst’s movement with swallowing and tongue protrusion is a hallmark feature.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Brachial cyst: Brachial cysts are usually found lateral to the midline, most commonly in the anterior triangle of the neck, and do not move with deglutition or tongue protrusion.

 

Option C. Plunging ranula: A plunging ranula originates from the floor of the mouth and extends into the neck. It is not typically a midline structure, nor does it move with swallowing or tongue protrusion.

 

Option D. Dermoid cyst: Dermoid cysts can occur in the midline but generally do not move with deglutition or tongue protrusion, making them less likely than a thyroglossal cyst in this case.

 

Educational objective:

 

A thyroglossal cyst is a midline neck swelling that moves with deglutition and tongue protrusion due to its connection with the thyroglossal duct.

questions.stem: Cardiac dominance is decided by:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Posterior interventricular artery

 

Cardiac dominance is determined by which coronary artery gives rise to the posterior interventricular artery. This artery supplies the posterior interventricular groove. In most individuals, the posterior interventricular artery arises from the right coronary artery (right-dominant circulation). In left-dominant circulation, it arises from the circumflex branch of the left coronary artery. Thus, the artery that provides the posterior interventricular artery dictates cardiac dominance.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Anterior interventricular artery: This artery, also known as the left anterior descending artery (LAD), supplies the anterior part of the heart and does not determine cardiac dominance.

 

Option C. Right coronary artery: While the right coronary artery supplies the posterior interventricular artery in a right-dominant heart, the key determinant is which artery gives rise to the posterior interventricular artery, not the right coronary artery alone.

 

Option D. Left coronary artery: Similar to the right coronary artery, the left coronary artery can supply the posterior interventricular artery in left-dominant hearts. However, cardiac dominance is directly based on the artery supplying the posterior interventricular artery.

 

Educational objective:

 

Cardiac dominance is determined by which coronary artery gives rise to the posterior interventricular artery.

questions.stem: A tumor of the uncinate process of the pancreas affects which of the following vessels?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Superior mesenteric artery

 

A tumor of the uncinate process of the pancreas is most likely to affect the superior mesenteric artery. The uncinate process is an extension of the pancreas that lies behind the superior mesenteric vessels. As described, a tumor in this area can compress both the superior mesenteric vein and artery, since they pass just in front of the uncinate process. Compression of these vessels leads to complications related to blood flow in the gastrointestinal tract.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Portal vein: The portal vein is formed by the union of the superior mesenteric vein and the splenic vein behind the neck of the pancreas. While it may be affected by tumors in the head of the pancreas, a tumor of the uncinate process primarily affects the superior mesenteric artery and vein.

 

Option C. Common hepatic artery: The common hepatic artery arises from the celiac trunk and does not pass in close proximity to the uncinate process, making it unlikely to be affected by a tumor in this location.

 

Option D. Inferior mesenteric artery: The inferior mesenteric artery supplies the distal portion of the colon and is located much lower in the abdomen, far from the uncinate process, so it would not be affected by a tumor in this region.

 

Educational objective:

 

A tumor in the uncinate process of the pancreas is most likely to compress the superior mesenteric artery due to its anatomical location in relation to the uncinate process.

questions.stem: A patient presented with clinical features of ataxia and incoordination. This is due to thrombosis of which artery?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Superior cerebellar

 

Ataxia and incoordination are classic signs of cerebellar dysfunction. Thrombosis of the superior cerebellar artery results in damage to the cerebellum, leading to these clinical features. The superior cerebellar artery supplies the upper portion of the cerebellum, which is responsible for coordination and balance, and thrombosis in this artery causes ataxia and other cerebellar signs.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Posterior cerebral artery: This artery supplies the occipital lobe, responsible for vision, and does not primarily affect the cerebellum, so it does not cause ataxia or incoordination.

 

Option B. Middle cerebral artery: Thrombosis in the middle cerebral artery typically affects motor and sensory functions, particularly on the contralateral side of the body, but it does not lead to ataxia or cerebellar signs.

 

Option C. Internal carotid artery: The internal carotid artery primarily supplies the anterior and middle portions of the brain. Its thrombosis leads to hemispheric stroke symptoms, such as weakness or speech disturbances, but not cerebellar ataxia.

 

Educational objective:

 

Thrombosis of the superior cerebellar artery causes ataxia and incoordination by affecting the cerebellum, which is responsible for balance and coordination.
questions.stemHtml: A patient presented with clinical features of ataxia and incoordination. This is due to thrombosis of which artery?

questions.stem: Nerve of the anterior compartment of the thigh is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Femoral nerve

 

The femoral nerve supplies the muscles of the anterior compartment of the thigh. This nerve is responsible for the motor supply to muscles such as the quadriceps femoris, which are essential for extending the leg at the knee joint. Additionally, the femoral nerve provides sensory innervation to the skin over the anterior and medial thigh. Its primary role is in movement and sensation for the anterior part of the thigh.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Obturator nerve: This nerve supplies the medial compartment of the thigh, primarily innervating the adductor muscles, not the anterior compartment.

 

Option C. Sciatic nerve: The sciatic nerve supplies the posterior compartment of the thigh, including muscles such as the hamstrings. It does not innervate the anterior compartment.

 

Option D. Tibial nerve: The tibial nerve is a branch of the sciatic nerve and primarily supplies the muscles of the posterior leg, not the anterior thigh.

 

Educational objective:

 

The femoral nerve is the primary nerve supplying the anterior compartment of the thigh, responsible for leg extension and sensory innervation of the anterior thigh.

questions.stem: A patient presented with the extension of MCP joint and flexion of IP joints. Which muscle is affected?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Interossei and lumbricals

 

The clinical sign of extension of the MCP joint and flexion of the IP joints is indicative of a "claw hand" deformity. This condition occurs when the lumbricals and interossei muscles are affected. These muscles normally flex the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints and extend the interphalangeal (IP) joints. When they are paralyzed, the extensor digitorum extends the MCP joints unchecked, while the flexors dominate at the IP joints, leading to flexion

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Extensor digitorum: This muscle extends both the MCP and IP joints, but its dysfunction would not lead to the claw hand deformity described.

 

Option C. Abductor pollicis: This muscle is responsible for abduction of the thumb and is not involved in the movement of the fingers or the claw hand deformity.

 

Option D. Abductor pollicis brevis: This muscle also affects thumb movement, specifically abduction, and does not play a role in MCP or IP joint movement.

 

Educational objective:

 

The interossei and lumbricals are responsible for flexing the MCP joints and extending the IP joints. Their dysfunction leads to the "claw hand" deformity.

questions.stem: The long left recurrent laryngeal nerve is due to the persistence of which arch artery?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) 6th arch

 

The long left recurrent laryngeal nerve is due to the persistence of the 6th arch artery. During embryological development, the recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks around the 6th arch artery on the left side. The ligamentum arteriosum, which is a remnant of the 6th arch, helps maintain this configuration. On the right side, the corresponding artery disappears, which explains why the right recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks around the right subclavian artery instead. Therefore, the 6th arch artery is crucial in forming the pathway for the left recurrent laryngeal nerve.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. 3rd arch: The 3rd arch artery contributes to the formation of the common carotid and part of the internal carotid artery, not related to the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

 

Option B. 4th arch: The 4th arch artery gives rise to parts of the aorta and subclavian artery, but it is not directly responsible for the pathway of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve.

 

Option C. 5th arch: The 5th arch is either absent or rudimentary in human development, playing no role in the pathway of the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

 

Educational objective:

 

The long left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops around the 6th arch artery, which plays a key role in its embryological development.

questions.stem: SSA fibres are present in which of the following cranial nerves?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) I, II, VIII

 

SSA (Special Somatic Afferent) fibers are present in cranial nerves I, II, and VIII. These fibers are involved in special senses like vision, hearing, and balance. Cranial nerve I (olfactory) is responsible for smell, cranial nerve II (optic) is responsible for vision, and cranial nerve VIII (vestibulocochlear) is responsible for hearing and balance. SSA fibers do not exist in cranial nerve VII, which is primarily involved in facial expression and taste.

 

Note - Cranial nerve VII (facial) does not contain SSA fibers. It is involved in motor function and the sense of taste but not in vision, hearing, or balance.

 

Educational objective:

 

SSA fibers are found in cranial nerves I, II, and VIII, which are involved in special senses like vision, hearing, and balance.

questions.stem: Which of the following cranial nerves' nuclei shows SSA features?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) VIII

 

The SSA (Special Somatic Afferent) fibers are present in cranial nerve VIII. These fibers are responsible for special senses such as hearing and balance. The nucleus associated with cranial nerve VIII is involved in processing these sensory inputs, making it the only cranial nerve in this list that contains SSA fibers with nuclei. Cranial nerves I and II have SSA fibers but do not possess a nucleus, as they are extensions of the brain.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. I: While cranial nerve I carries SSA fibers responsible for smell, it does not have an associated nucleus.

 

Option B. II: Cranial nerve II carries SSA fibers responsible for vision, but like cranial nerve I, it does not have an associated nucleus.

 

Option C. VII: Cranial nerve VII is primarily a motor nerve and is not involved in special somatic afferent functions.

 

Educational objective:

 

Cranial nerve VIII, which handles hearing and balance, is the only nerve in this list that has SSA fibers and an associated nucleus.

questions.stem: GSE fibers are present in:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) III, IV, VI, XII

 

GSE (General Somatic Efferent) fibers are responsible for motor control of skeletal muscles, particularly those involved in eye and tongue movement. These fibers are found in cranial nerves III (oculomotor), IV (trochlear), VI (abducens), and XII (hypoglossal). These cranial nerves innervate the extraocular muscles (III, IV, and VI) and the muscles of the tongue (XII), contributing to movements such as eye movement and tongue positioning.

 

Note:

 

I and II: Cranial nerves I (olfactory) and II (optic) do not contain GSE fibers, as they are sensory nerves responsible for smell and vision.

 

Educational objective:

 

GSE fibers are present in cranial nerves III, IV, VI, and XII, which are involved in controlling eye and tongue movements.

questions.stem: Which of the following are branches of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery? Superior gluteal arteryInferior gluteal arterySuperior vesical arteryMiddle rectal arteryInferior vesical arteryVaginal artery
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) 2, 3, 4, 5, 6

 

The anterior division of the internal iliac artery gives rise to several branches, including the inferior gluteal artery, superior vesical artery, middle rectal artery, inferior vesical artery, and vaginal artery. These arteries supply various pelvic and perineal structures.

 

On the other hand, the superior gluteal artery arises from the posterior division of the internal iliac artery.

 

Educational objective:

 

The anterior division of the internal iliac artery includes branches such as the inferior gluteal artery, superior vesical artery, middle rectal artery, inferior vesical artery, and vaginal artery.

questions.stemHtml: Fibers from the marked structure end in which of the following areas of the thalamus?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Anterior nucleus

 

The marked structure in the image is the mammillary body, which is a part of the Papez circuit. Fibers from the mammillary body travel through the mammillothalamic tract to reach the anterior nucleus of the thalamus. This pathway is crucial for memory processing and is part of the limbic system's communication network.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Posterior nucleus: This nucleus is involved in pain and temperature sensation, not the Papez circuit.

 

Option B. Reticular nucleus: The reticular nucleus modulates thalamic activity but does not receive input from the mammillary body.

 

Option D. Ventral Lateral nucleus: This nucleus is associated with motor control, and it does not receive fibers from the mammillary body.

 

Educational objective:

 

Fibers from the mammillary body travel to the anterior nucleus of the thalamus as part of the Papez circuit, which is involved in memory processing.

questions.stemHtml: A 48-year-old female patient presented with recurrent episodes of severe abdominal pain, which is often accompanied by nausea and vomiting. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy reveals multiple peptic ulcers in the duodenal bulb. Laboratory tests show elevated gastrin levels. She was given Prilosec for a long time. She was also consuming a vegetarian diet and now presented with tiredness & palpitations since a month. She complained of progressive sensory loss in her lower extremities. Neurological examination reveals impaired vibratory sensation in both legs. An MRI of the spinal cord shows no structural abnormalities. On blood examination, the following hematological slide was found. All of the following statements are correct in this case except:

options.label: A
options.text: This is a case of gastrinoma with high gastrin secretion resulting in hypersecretion of hydrochloric acid.

options.label: B
options.text: Prilosec is an example of a proton pump inhibitor which may cause decreased Vitamin B12 absorption.

options.label: C
options.text: In this patient due to Vitamin B12 deficiency, myelination of the anterior spinothalamic tract has been affected.

options.label: D
options.text: On hematological examination, increased mean corpuscular volume (MCV >100 fL) and mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH) and polymorphonuclear cells with multiple lobes are found.

questions.answerText: In this patient due to Vitamin B12 deficiency, myelination of the anterior spinothalamic tract has been affected.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) In this patient due to Vitamin B12 deficiency, myelination of the anterior spinothalamic tract has been affected.

 

The patient’s condition is due to gastrinoma, which causes high levels of gastrin and leads to hypersecretion of hydrochloric acid, resulting in multiple peptic ulcers. The use of Prilosec, a proton pump inhibitor, over a long period can cause malabsorption of Vitamin B12, especially in a vegetarian diet, as this patient followed. A deficiency in Vitamin B12 is known to affect myelination in the dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis and fasciculus cuneatus), which are responsible for proprioception and vibratory sensations. In this case, vibratory sensation is impaired, pointing to involvement of the dorsal columns, not the anterior spinothalamic tract, which is responsible for pain and temperature sensation.

 

The hematological findings, such as increased MCV and hypersegmented neutrophils, are classic signs of megaloblastic anemia caused by Vitamin B12 deficiency.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. This is a case of gastrinoma with high gastrin secretion resulting in hypersecretion of hydrochloric acid: This statement is correct, as gastrinoma leads to elevated gastrin levels and results in excessive acid production, causing peptic ulcers.

 

Option B. Prilosec is an example of a proton pump inhibitor which may cause decreased Vitamin B12 absorption: This statement is correct, as prolonged use of proton pump inhibitors such as Prilosec can interfere with Vitamin B12 absorption.

 

Option D. On haematological examination, increased mean corpuscular volume (MCV >100 fL) and mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH) and polymorphonuclear cells with multiple lobes are found: This is also correct, as these findings are characteristic of megaloblastic anemia, which is commonly caused by Vitamin B12 deficiency.

 

Educational objective:

 

Vitamin B12 deficiency leads to myelination defects primarily in the dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis and fasciculus cuneatus), not the anterior spinothalamic tract.

questions.stemHtml: A 21-year-old null gravida Caucasian patient presented with a 15-month history of amenorrhea, bifrontal headache, and photophobia. Examination revealed general physical, neurologic, and ophthalmoscopic findings with normal visual fields. A pelvic examination revealed normal external genitalia, nulliparous cervix and uterus, and bilateral cystic ovarian masses measuring 8 cm in diameter on the right and 4 cm on the left. Endocrine evaluation revealed an elevated serum prolactin in the range of 48 to 50 ng/ml. This situation was related with mass in the following area of the below image:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) B

 

The patient’s elevated serum prolactin and bilateral cystic ovarian masses are indicative of a prolactinoma, a type of pituitary adenoma that causes hyperprolactinemia. this condition leads to menstrual disturbances such as amenorrhea, as seen in this patient. The mass responsible for the condition is located in the pituitary gland, which resides in the sella turcica (Turkish saddle), marked as area B in the image. The pituitary gland secretes prolactin, and a tumor in this region leads to excessive hormone secretion, 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. A: This area represents the crista galli, a bony ridge in the anterior cranial fossa. It is not related to the pituitary gland or prolactin secretion.

 

Option C. C: This area corresponds to the internal acoustic meatus, which is involved in auditory and vestibular functions. It has no relation to pituitary adenomas or prolactin secretion.

 

Option D. D: This area marks the foramen magnum, which is the opening in the skull through which the spinal cord passes. It is not related to the pituitary gland or prolactinoma.

 

Educational objective:

 

A prolactinoma, located in the pituitary gland (in the sella turcica), can cause elevated serum prolactin levels, amenorrhea, and ovarian cysts.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the marked structure:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Accessory nerve

 

The accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI) is responsible for innervating the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles. This nerve runs across the posterior triangle of the neck, it can be identified due to its position along the path associated with these muscles. The accessory nerve typically crosses the posterior triangle in an oblique direction, making it distinguishable in this region.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Transverse cervical nerve: This nerve provides sensory innervation to the skin of the anterior neck. It does not follow the same path as the accessory nerve and would be located in a different region of the neck.

 

Option B. Lesser occipital nerve: This nerve runs along the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle and innervates the skin of the neck and scalp behind the ear. Its location does not match the nerve marked in the image.

 

Option C. Great auricular nerve: This nerve supplies sensation to the skin over the parotid gland and the auricle. It typically ascends vertically along the sternocleidomastoid muscle, but its location does not correspond to the marked structure in the image.

 

Educational objective:

 

The accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI) runs through the posterior triangle of the neck, innervating the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles.
